section_summary: This section documents U.S. monitoring of Japanese propaganda, intelligence, espionage, and fifth-column activity from 1940 through early 1942. It includes intercepted Japanese correspondence, reports on overseas radio broadcasts and covert organizations targeting Overseas Chinese, descriptions of Japanese military and naval intelligence structures, and FBI warnings shared with the State, War, and Navy Departments. Later papers address Japanese strategic aims, Axis tensions over Asian resources, and ideological themes in Japanese wartime publications.

subfiles.title: Memorandum transmitting intercepted Japanese propaganda correspondence
subfiles.from: Colonel J. T. H. O'Hara, G-2
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Transmits British-provided translations of intercepted Japanese consular correspondence concerning propaganda and intelligence activity in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: O'Hara forwards four translated Japanese letters intercepted by British censors and supplied through the British Consul General in Manila. He states that the letters demonstrate the breadth of Japanese propaganda and intelligence organization.

subfiles.title: Request to investigate distribution of propaganda materials
subfiles.from: Matsudaira Tadahisa, Acting Consul General, Canton
subfiles.about: Requests an investigation of the receipt, distribution, and reception of propaganda sent to Overseas Chinese.
subfiles.summary: At the request of the Japanese Army's intelligence-information section in South China, Matsudaira asks the Singapore consulate to trace propaganda materials sent to named Overseas Chinese. Equivalent requests were being sent to Japanese establishments in Hong Kong, Hanoi, Batavia, Manila, and Saigon.

subfiles.title: Distribution of Wang Ching-wei gramophone records
subfiles.about: Announces shipment and planned distribution of recordings of a Wang Ching-wei broadcast.
subfiles.summary: The sender distributes gramophone records of Wang Ching-wei's August 9 speech, “Now Peace Can Be Materialised,” for circulation among Chinese residents. Allotments are listed for Japanese posts across Southeast Asia and in San Francisco and New York.

subfiles.title: Investigation regarding distribution of propaganda articles
subfiles.about: Reports on the arrival and effectiveness of Japanese propaganda among Overseas Chinese.
subfiles.summary: Nagao reports that the materials appear to have reached their destinations and notes increasing Overseas Chinese interest in occupied territories and Wang Ching-wei's peace movement. He recommends continued distribution but warns that crude attacks on Chiang Kai-shek may alienate Chinese readers and provoke confiscation by local governments.

subfiles.title: Request for investigation of printed propaganda distribution
subfiles.from: Yoshida Kijiro, Army Information Section, South China
subfiles.about: Asks officials to determine whether mailed Japanese propaganda reached selected Overseas Chinese recipients and how they reacted.
subfiles.summary: Yoshida explains that propaganda was mailed directly to educators, influential people, anti-Japanese leaders, newspaper offices, and writers. Because the Army was unsure whether it arrived, he requests an investigation of both distribution and audience reaction.

subfiles.title: American Embassy Memorandum No. 216 on the Nippon Trade Agency
subfiles.about: Reports that the Nippon Trade Agency served Japanese propaganda and clandestine communications functions.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the agency paid press outlets, propagandists, and other persons abroad. Secret documents were to be held by consuls, while nonbusiness messages were carried by ship captains or special messengers; a worldwide list of agency branches is appended.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Colonel Churchill on the Nippon Trade Agency
subfiles.about: Shares intelligence that the Nippon Trade Agency acted as a Japanese propaganda and clandestine-message network.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum repeats a confidential report on secret documents being stored with Japanese consuls and messages being carried by ships' captains or special couriers. It lists branches around the world and notes parallel dissemination to Naval Intelligence and the FBI.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Captain Nixon on the Nippon Trade Agency
subfiles.to: Captain Nixon, Office of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Provides Naval Intelligence with the confidential report on the Nippon Trade Agency's propaganda and communications role.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes consular custody of secret papers and use of special messengers or ship captains for sensitive traffic. A global branch list is supplied, with notice that the same information went to Military Intelligence and the FBI.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for Mr. Tamm on the Nippon Trade Agency
subfiles.to: Mr. Tamm, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Provides the FBI with information on the Nippon Trade Agency's alleged Japanese propaganda activities and secret communications.
subfiles.summary: The document repeats the report that agency branches supported Japanese propaganda and held clandestine papers with local consuls. It lists branches in the Americas, Europe, Africa, and Asia and records distribution to Army and Navy intelligence.

subfiles.title: Request for cooperation with foreign propaganda
subfiles.about: Solicits cooperation in expanding and assessing Japanese propaganda abroad, including in Central and South America.
subfiles.summary: The heavily damaged page identifies the text as a translated, possibly intercepted letter concerning cooperation with foreign propaganda. It calls for use of the circulated material and reports on public reaction, with Central and South America specifically mentioned.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Organization of a new Cabinet Intelligence Bureau
subfiles.about: Refers researchers to another file concerning the organization of a new Japanese Cabinet Intelligence Bureau.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a report from Ambassador Grew in Japan dated September 21, 1940. The original was filed under 894.002/440.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Establishment of the new Intelligence Bureau
subfiles.about: Points to a report outlining the organization of Japan's newly established Intelligence Bureau.
subfiles.summary: This file note refers to Grew's December 12, 1940 report on establishment of the new Intelligence Bureau. The original was placed in file 894.002/447.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division routing form
subfiles.to: Internal War Department and interagency distribution list
subfiles.about: Provides a circulation and disposition form for intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: The page lists War Department branches, armed-services offices, military schools, and other government recipients. It contains no substantive narrative beyond instructions to note, return, or forward the associated material.

subfiles.title: Comments on Current Events No. 5: Intensified Japanese Radio Propaganda
subfiles.from: Hawaiian Department, Fort Shafter; signed for the Commanding General by Major Carl Grosse
subfiles.about: Analyzes the expansion, content, and possible effects of Japanese radio propaganda directed at Hawaii and worldwide audiences.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Japan's expanded 34-hour overseas broadcasting schedule, its languages and target regions, and the intensive exposure of Hawaii's Japanese community to Tokyo programming. It summarizes speeches by Yosuke Matsuoka, Shigeshi Nagata, and Admiral Suetsugu promoting Japanese nationalism, the Greater East Asia sphere, and resistance to the United States and Britain. It also reviews George Nakamoto's English-language commentary on American politics and U.S. defenses at Guam, Cavite, and the Philippines.

subfiles.title: FBI letter on reorganization of the Tokyo propaganda bureau
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports German-assisted reorganization and expansion of Japanese foreign-language broadcasting.
subfiles.summary: Hoover states that the Tokyo Bureau of Propaganda was reportedly being reorganized under German Propaganda Ministry direction. Shinroku Tanomogi was expected to direct shortwave broadcasts in sixteen languages, using native speakers and Japan Broadcasting Company networks.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on alleged Domei subversion in Indochina, Thailand, and Mexico
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Relays an allegation that Domei News representatives were conducting subversive work abroad.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum quotes a February 23 letter written in Manila by an American Philippine Government employee. Former French consul Gaston Willoquet reportedly said that Indochinese authorities regarded the Domei representative Ata as an agent who undermined native loyalty in Indochina and Thailand, while another Domei representative performed similar work in Mexico.

subfiles.title: FBI letter on photographic secret messages
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports an unconfirmed method allegedly used by Japanese agents to transmit secret photographic messages.
subfiles.summary: An outside confidential source claimed Japanese agents used a photographic process producing writing that became undeveloped or disappeared when exposed to light. Hoover emphasizes that the report was unconfirmed but potentially useful and copies Army and Navy intelligence.

subfiles.title: Exposure of the Chung Woh Company as a Japanese–Wang Ching-wei fifth-column organization
subfiles.from: K. S. Patton, American Consul General, Singapore
subfiles.about: Reports police findings on a Hong Kong-based propaganda, espionage, sabotage, and subversion organization operating under commercial cover.
subfiles.summary: Patton describes the Chung Woh, Chin Kee, Ban Chung Woh, and Wing Kee names as covers for a Japanese-connected Wang Ching-wei organization exposed by Hong Kong police raids. Its open and secret branches allegedly targeted Overseas Chinese, collected military intelligence, encouraged sabotage and anticolonial rebellion, attacked the Kuomintang and Communists, and sought branches throughout Southeast Asia. The despatch also summarizes its failed attempt to form an effective Malayan branch and stresses the need to protect informants and agent lists.

subfiles.title: Overseas Works of the East Asiatic Chain of Co-Prosperity
subfiles.to: Enclosure to the Singapore consular despatch
subfiles.about: Charts a Hong Kong-directed network and its proposed activities in the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: The chart places a general company in Hong Kong above branches at Medan, Surabaya, and Batavia. Assigned work includes inciting independence movements, sabotage, attacks on military and police forces, collecting political, economic, and military information, and spreading inflammatory propaganda.

subfiles.title: Partial list of agents of the National Salvation Through Peace Society
subfiles.to: Enclosure to the Singapore consular despatch
subfiles.about: Lists names and aliases associated with the alleged Japanese–Wang Ching-wei fifth-column organization.
subfiles.summary: The damaged list identifies several agents or aliases connected with Hong Kong, Saigon, and Malaya. Legible names include Tse Hung Yi, King Chung, Chan Kit alias Cha Man Wing, Hung King Man, and Chong Poe Tong.

subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report: Japanese Espionage Training
subfiles.from: Lieutenant Colonel J. K. Evans, G-2
subfiles.about: Reports that a Japanese commercial employee attended a suspected propaganda and espionage school while visiting Japan.
subfiles.summary: According to Hong Kong British Intelligence, a Japanese employee of a Surabaya firm wrote that he was attending an institute staffed by Army, Navy, and Overseas Affairs Ministry instructors. The school was believed to be one of Japan's “Southward Expansion” centers for training colonists in propaganda and espionage; the Netherlands East Indies government canceled the man's temporary residence permit.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Japanese fifth column in Malaya
subfiles.about: Refers to excerpts from a War Department circular concerning a Japanese fifth column in Malaya.
subfiles.summary: The note directs researchers to a Navy Department letter dated January 13, 1942. The original was filed under 862.20000/52.

subfiles.title: FBI inquiry concerning Sakae Nihara
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests any State Department information concerning the Japanese national Sakae Nihara.
subfiles.summary: Hoover asks the Department to search its records for Sakae Nihara. The letter provides two last-known addresses in Tokyo's Azabu district.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning Sakae Nihara
subfiles.about: Reports that State Department files contained no record of Sakae Nihara.
subfiles.summary: The reply refers to Hoover's January 27 inquiry. It states succinctly that the Department has no record of the individual.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of memorandum on the Japanese Intelligence Service
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a confidential memorandum describing the Japanese Intelligence Service.
subfiles.summary: Hoover encloses a February 6 memorandum based on an outside confidential and reliable source. Copies were also furnished to Rear Admiral T. S. Wilkinson and Brigadier General Raymond E. Lee.

subfiles.title: Japanese Intelligence Service
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation confidential source
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation and intelligence recipients
subfiles.about: Describes the organization, methods, personnel, and political functions of Japanese military, naval, consular, commercial, and secret-society intelligence.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum portrays Japanese espionage as a pervasive national obligation supported by private citizens, commercial firms, attachés, consulates, military special services, and the China Affairs Board. It emphasizes the Army Special Service's political intrigue, subversion, propaganda, and preparation of occupied territories, while distinguishing the Navy's greater focus on naval information. It also describes the planting of trained agents in firms, news agencies, and consulates and the use of commercial associations and secret societies as government cover.

subfiles.title: FBI letter on Japanese intelligence collection priorities
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Lists economic, industrial, labor, shipping, and supply information sought by Japanese intelligence agents.
subfiles.summary: Japanese agents were reportedly ordered to collect data on armament production, shipping, labor and transportation, ship construction and losses, raw-material consumption, food supplies, and substitute materials. The requirements applied not only to the United States and Great Britain but also to Germany and Italy, with Spanish communications expected to carry reports where Japanese embassies no longer operated.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of memorandum on Japanese strategy
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential-source information concerning Japanese wartime strategy.
subfiles.summary: Hoover sends an attached strategic memorandum for State Department consideration. He notes that it was also supplied to William J. Donovan, T. S. Wilkinson, and Hayes A. Kroner.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on German–Japanese tensions and Japanese strategy
subfiles.to: Federal Bureau of Investigation and interagency recipients
subfiles.about: Assesses Axis disagreements over Asian resources and possible Japanese moves toward India and Madagascar.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports German pressure for access to tin, rubber, and other resources seized by Japan in the Indies and Malaya, together with German resentment that Japan was benefiting from German victories. It suggests that competition over India could strain the partnership and help explain Japanese concentration in that direction rather than on Australia. Comparing French Indochina to Czechoslovakia, it warns that Madagascar might become a similar Japanese bridgehead and submarine base threatening Allied communications and the Atlantic.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on five Japanese propaganda books
subfiles.about: Summarizes reviews of five Japanese books illustrating wartime propaganda and ideological thought.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum says the books assume German victory, blame the democracies' economic selfishness for the world crisis, and portray Japan's Axis-aligned program as a spiritual and divine mission for world peace and racial order. The works denounce liberalism, democracy, Christianity, Communism, socialism, unionism, humanitarianism, and Margaret Sanger while advocating an East Asian co-prosperity sphere encompassing Australia, New Zealand, and India. They also explain the prolonged war in China through Japanese unpreparedness, insufficient domestic seriousness, Chinese hostility, and third-power aid.
